source.title_on_document: Who Thinks First? Designing Productive Friction with Engage-to-Unlock GenAI

supplement.where: Appendices A-E, pp. 26-31 of this PDF. No separately hosted supplementary material or online appendix is identified in the document.
supplement.holds: Appendix A contains Table 3 demographics; Appendix B contains Figure 6 task-duration distributions; Appendix C contains Figure 7 lexical-frequency profiles with SEM bands; Appendix D reproduces the assistant prompts; Appendix E gives a sample conversation. No additional tables of discourse contrast SEs or CIs are included, despite the reporting statement on p. 8.

paper_design_summary: Prolific participants wrote an argumentative essay with no AI, immediate generative chatbot access, engagement-gated access, or time-matched access; only the first three conditions were randomly assigned, while the time-matched condition was recruited in a separate phase (pp. 5-7). The final essays were scored for semantic dispersion, semantic location, lexical reuse, length, and argumentative structure, with a separately generated AI-only reference corpus (pp. 8-9, 12-15). The same participants then evaluated source-based passages without AI; this assessed error detection and classification rather than creative production (pp. 7 and 10).

studies.label: Argumentative writing experiment with a randomized first phase and a nonrandom time-matched cohort

assignment.what_was_assigned: Phase 1 participants were randomly assigned to Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, or Engage-to-Unlock. A separately recruited Phase 2 sample, excluding Phase 1 participants, was assigned entirely to Time-Matched Unlock and yoked to recorded Engage-to-Unlock schedules. Thus online_rct applies to comparisons among the three Phase 1 arms only; any contrast involving Time-Matched Unlock is quasi_people (observational context), not randomized. The AI-only reference was not assigned to people or an experimental arm.
assignment.quote: In Phase 1, participants were randomly assigned to Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, or Engage-to-Unlock. In Phase 2, all participants were assigned to Time-Matched Unlock.
assignment.locator: p. 6, sections 3.1-3.2; p. 20, section 5.3 explicitly limits randomized comparisons to Phase 1; p. 8, section 3.5.3 (AI-only reference)

arms.name: Human-Only
arms.description: Phase 1 randomized condition: wrote without an assistant; all conditions received the shared readings (pp. 6-7).

arms.name: Standard Chatbot
arms.description: Phase 1 randomized condition: Tell-me direct generative assistance available throughout writing (p. 6).

arms.name: Engage-to-Unlock
arms.description: Phase 1 randomized condition: Teach-me guidance available initially; Tell-me unlocked once the draft expressed a position and a distinct supporting argumentative development. Unlocking did not automatically switch modes (p. 6).

arms.name: Time-Matched Unlock
arms.description: Nonrandom Phase 2 condition: Teach-me initially, with Tell-me access scheduled to match an earlier Engage-to-Unlock participant regardless of the current draft. Some scheduled unlocks were not delivered (pp. 6 and 11).

participants.exclusions: Of 445 session completers, 398 passed both embedded attention checks and entered the final analysis; numbers originally assigned and pre-exclusion arm counts are not reported (p. 6). Six internal pilot sessions were excluded from the main analysis (p. 7). Analyses retained the attention-check-passing participants with unlock-delivery deviations (p. 8); the timer problem affected 14 Time-Matched Unlock participants (p. 11). The analysis follows attention-check exclusions; the paper does not establish that every randomized participant was retained.
participants.who: Prolific participants in five English-speaking countries, paid $30 for an approximately one-hour study; age range 19-76, mean 35.7 years (SD 11.5); 97.5% held an undergraduate degree (p. 6).
participants.country: Canada; India; South Africa; United Kingdom; United States
participants.quote: Of 445 respondents who completed the session, 398 passed two embedded attention checks and were included in the final analysis
participants.locator: p. 6, section 3.2; p. 26, Table 3; pp. 7-8 (pilot exclusion and sample inclusion); p. 11, section 4.1.1 (unlock deviation)

ai_tool.how_used: A conversational writing assistant could see the live essay, conversation history, and reference sources. Tell-me could supply ideas, reasoning, organization, revisions, and draft prose; Teach-me offered process guidance and was instructed not to supply substantive topic-specific content. Standard Chatbot used Tell-me throughout; the other assisted arms began with Teach-me and could later switch to Tell-me (pp. 5-6 and 26-29). AI remained available during writing as guidance even when direct generation was never unlocked: 98 of 107 Engage-to-Unlock participants and 60 of 94 Time-Matched Unlock participants received Tell-me access before submission (p. 11).

task.description: Task 1: write at least 200 words about the four-day workweek using four source summaries, two supportive and two critical, with source order counterbalanced. The essay task qualifies through its across-writer diversity measure; no human-rated overall creativity or novelty outcome is reported. Task 2 subsequently required evaluating eight 150-word AI-generated passages without AI; it was an error-evaluation task, not a further creative-writing task (p. 7).
task.duration: Each task had a suggested duration of 20 minutes, but participants worked at their own pace; study approximately one hour (pp. 6-7).

outcomes.name: Within-condition semantic dispersion (D_c), with homogenization index (HI_c)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean squared Euclidean distance of complete final-essay embeddings from their condition centroid. HI_c = 1 - D_c / D_Human-Only is a rescaling of the same outcome, retained here rather than counted separately. Embeddings have 3,072 dimensions. The four participant conditions are the four sets counted in n_units; the AI-only reference is described separately in notes. Methods: p. 9, section 3.5.3; results: p. 13, Table 1 and section 4.2.1.

contrasts.reported: Standard Chatbot: n = 98, D_c = 0.188 [0.178, 0.194], HI_c = -0.050 (-5.0%); Human-Only: n = 99, D_c = 0.179 [0.167, 0.188], HI_c = 0.000 (baseline). Brackets are within-condition 95% bootstrap CIs. The treatment point estimate is higher, but the paper presents dispersion descriptively and does not test a between-condition difference or equivalence.

diversity_detail.metric: D_c = mean squared Euclidean distance to the condition centroid; HI_c = 1 - D_c / D_Human-Only.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Gemini Embedding 2; 3,072-dimensional vectors; SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY task type (p. 9, section 3.5.3).
diversity_detail.computed_over: One complete final essay per writer, compared with the centroid of the essays in that same condition after whitespace normalization. This is dispersion across different writers, not variation within one writer (p. 9, section 3.5.3).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Within-condition 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals from 5,000 resamples. The resampling unit is not explicitly identified beyond the essay-based dispersion calculation. No bootstrap interval for the arm difference, participant-level contrast SE, or formal difference/equivalence test is supplied (pp. 9 and 13).
diversity_detail.notes: Larger D_c means greater diversity. Larger HI_c means greater homogenization, so its interpretation is reversed for an atlas effect favoring diversity; no effect or sign-transformed number was computed. The no_clear_difference codes reflect the descriptive analysis and absence of a formal contrast, not evidence of equivalence. The text explicitly distinguishes PCA location from diversity (p. 9).

outcomes.name: Total number of discourse elements
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: An LLM-based discourse classifier counts argumentative discourse elements in each final essay (p. 8, section 3.5.3). The categories are Lead, Position, Claim, Counterclaim, Rebuttal, Evidence, and Concluding Statement (p. 6, section 3.1). Counts are structural elements, not independently generated ideas or an overall creativity rating. The classifier model is not separately identified.

contrasts.reported: Mean discourse-element counts: Standard Chatbot 9.71, Human-Only 8.30. Exploratory ordinary ANOVA across all four participant conditions: F(3, 394) = 4.66, p = .003. The direction is descriptive; this omnibus test does not establish a significant Standard Chatbot versus Human-Only difference. No SD or pair-specific test is printed.

Mean counts: Engage-to-Unlock 9.66, Standard Chatbot 9.71. Four-condition omnibus F(3, 394) = 4.66, p = .003. The text says contrasts for the remaining discourse outcomes were not statistically significant; exact pairwise statistics are not printed.

Nonrandom comparison: Time-Matched Unlock was recruited in Phase 2, separately from the Phase 1 comparator (p. 6, sections 3.1-3.2; p. 20, section 5.3). Mean counts: Engage-to-Unlock 9.66, Time-Matched Unlock 9.16. Four-condition omnibus F(3, 394) = 4.66, p = .003. The text says contrasts for the remaining discourse outcomes were not statistically significant; exact pairwise statistics are not printed.

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct discourse categories present in a participant's final essay, range 0-7, derived by the LLM discourse classifier (p. 8, section 3.5.3). Coded as within-person category variety (flexibility), not across-person diversity. These are rhetorical categories rather than categories of independently generated ideas; no category-diversity means, SDs, exact p-values, SEs, or intervals are printed.

outcomes.question: with_ai

outcomes.name: Semantic location of essays (joint PCA component scores)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Exploratory joint PCA of L2-normalized embeddings from participant and AI-only essays (498 essays; p. 9, section 3.5.3). Components are retained together as the semantic-location analysis. The paper explicitly says PCA measures location rather than diversity. PC1 explains 17.91% of variance; PC2 4.44%; PC3 3.61%. Five-corpus omnibus tests: PC1 F(4, 493) = 255.62, p < .001; PC2 F(4, 493) = 0.56, p = .693; PC3 F(4, 493) = 13.59, p < .001 (p. 12, Figure 2). PCA coordinate direction has no inherent better-creativity interpretation. t-SNE is visualization only, not another diversity endpoint.

contrasts.reported: PC1 centroids: Engage-to-Unlock M = -0.090; Standard Chatbot M = -0.014; p_Holm < .001. Human-Only M = -0.122 and AI-only M = +0.291 provide descriptive reference locations. The remaining tested components did not show significant planned differences. Omnibus PCA tests are reported in Figure 2, but contrast SEs and intervals are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 14, section 4.2.1; p. 12, Figure 2; p. 9, section 3.5.3

contrasts.reported: Nonrandom comparison: Time-Matched Unlock was recruited in Phase 2, separately from the Phase 1 comparator (p. 6, sections 3.1-3.2; p. 20, section 5.3). PC1 centroids: Engage-to-Unlock M = -0.090; Time-Matched Unlock M = -0.065; p_Holm = .104. Contrasts on remaining components also did not detect significant differences.

outcomes.name: Normalized content-word frequency profiles
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Descriptive vocabulary profiles for the 85 most frequent content words in Human-Only. Alphabetic tokens are lowercased; single-character tokens and closed-class stopwords are excluded. Each token count is divided by total essay word count and multiplied by 1,000. Figure 7 plots condition means and +/-1 SEM across essays. This is word usage, not a direct cross-person diversity statistic. No numerical token-level table or hypothesis tests are supplied (p. 9, section 3.5.3; p. 28, Appendix C, Figure 7). The figure does not separately state its analyzed essay count; n_units is therefore null.

contrasts.reported: Figure 7 plots the Standard Chatbot and Human-Only frequency profiles. The text notes that several words especially frequent in AI-only essays were also more frequent in AI-assisted essays than Human-Only, but says shared topics and sources cannot be separated from AI assistance using this descriptive pattern. No plot values were estimated.
Engage-to-Unlock and Human-Only content-word frequency profiles are shown with +/-1 SEM; no separate numerical estimates or inferential test is printed.

Nonrandom comparison: Time-Matched Unlock was recruited in Phase 2, separately from the Phase 1 comparator (p. 6, sections 3.1-3.2; p. 20, section 5.3). Time-Matched Unlock and Human-Only content-word frequency profiles are shown with +/-1 SEM; no separate numerical estimates or inferential test is printed.

eligibility.reason: Phase 1 randomly assigned people to Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, and Engage-to-Unlock (p. 6, sections 3.1-3.2). The reported analyzed arm counts are 99, 98, and 107, respectively, so the randomized comparison arms themselves exceed the 50-person criterion; the overall analyzed count of 398 also includes 94 nonrandom Phase 2 participants and must not be called randomized (p. 6; p. 26, Table 3). Final-essay semantic dispersion compares outputs across different writers and is reported by arm with bootstrap CIs (p. 9, section 3.5.3; p. 13, Table 1). Only Phase 1 contrasts qualify as randomized evidence. Time-Matched Unlock comparisons are nonrandom, and the AI-only corpus is descriptive context. Core eligibility rests on across_people, not on the later passage-evaluation task or ancillary writing metrics.

one_line_finding: Among 398 analyzed writers, within-condition semantic dispersion was descriptively similar (D_c = 0.179-0.188; p. 13, Table 1), with no formal test of between-condition differences or equivalence (p. 9, section 3.5.3).
open_questions: Numbers originally randomized, phase-specific pre-exclusion counts, and arm-specific attention-check exclusions are not reported; the 445 figure is session completers, not a randomized count (p. 6).

The methods promise discourse contrast means, SEs and CIs (p. 8), but the results and included appendices do not supply them for most discourse outcomes. No external supplement or data/code location is stated.

Dispersion is reported with within-condition bootstrap intervals but without contrast precision or a formal difference test. A usable diversity contrast SE cannot be extracted from the printed table (pp. 9 and 13).
notes: One study entry represents the paper's single two-phase experiment; the nonrandom second phase is explicitly identified in assignment and every affected contrast. The descriptive AI-only corpus is not an additional participant arm or an independent human study. It contains 100 independently generated essays (p. 8); Table 1 reports D_c = 0.065 [0.061, 0.068] and HI_c = +0.636 (+63.6%) versus Human-Only (p. 13). Its Table 2 length is 495.5 +/- 38.3 words, source coverage 2.03% +/- 1.59%, and source-match prevalence 74.0% (p. 15). These AI-versus-human reference numbers are context only. No reanalysis of another paper's experimental participants is stated; the PERSUADE 2.0 essays on p. 6 were used to validate the discourse classifier, not as participants in the experiment. All reported outcome values were checked against PDF text; the complete markdown, including references and appendices, was read. The twelve outcome entries retain the output-based writing measures, including ancillary semantic-location, vocabulary and reuse measures as other; those ancillary measures are not treated as creativity ratings or across-writer diversity. HI_c is grouped with dispersion and PCA components are grouped under semantic location. No additional unreported category-specific counts were inferred from the classifier's category list. Raw directions for text reuse denote the amount copied and do not assert a creativity benefit; PCA coordinates also have no creativity sign. For Match percentages, statistics_available is none because only descriptive proportions are supplied and the allowed vocabulary has no proportions-only category; the printed proportions remain in reported. AI-availability fields refer to assisted writing conditions; Human-Only has no AI, and both gated conditions have guidance throughout, regardless of generation-mode unlock. Inventory of other reported outcomes, outside this screening's creative-output questions: source/AI paste actions (p. 15, Table 2), prompt counts and mode usage (pp. 11-13), passage judgment/detection/classification and complete-diagnosis accuracy (pp. 10 and 15-16, Figure 3), their accuracy-per-time measures (pp. 16-17, Figure 4), writing/evaluation/total time and the task-by-condition interaction (pp. 16-18, Figure 5; p. 27, Figure 6), and self-reported agency, satisfaction, ownership, workload and disruption (pp. 10 and 18). Task 2 was after AI removal, but involved evaluating supplied passages rather than producing creative work or taking a convergent-creativity test, so it is not counted as an after_ai creativity outcome. The appendix also supplies demographics, system prompts and a conversation example (pp. 26-31); it adds no scored creative output or missing numerical discourse table. Preregistration and data/code URLs are not stated. No effect sizes or plot values were calculated.
